entries.title: Equality of Opportunity in Supervised Learning
entries.name: Equalized-odds postprocessing for binary predictors
entries.definition: A randomized postprocessing algorithm that uses a binary predictor and protected-group membership to minimize expected label loss subject to equal false-positive and true-positive rates across groups, within predictors derived from those inputs.
entries.mechanism: For binary groups and binary predictions, optimize four probabilities of outputting one, indexed by the original prediction and group. The joint distribution of original prediction, group and target supplies linear loss and parity constraints. The feasible group error-rate pairs form the convex hull of the original classifier, its complement and the two constant classifiers; their intersection supplies equalized-odds solutions. Prediction uses the original output and group, with randomization as needed.
entries.locator: Section 4, Definition 4.1 and Section 4.1, equations (4.1)–(4.3), Proposition 4.4, PDF pp. 5–7; Section 6 and Discussion for distributional limitations
entries.identity_notes: This record selects the Section 4.1 binary-input linear program. It is distinct from the EqualizedOdds criterion and from the continuous-score threshold construction in Section 4.2. Equal-opportunity-only constraints define a relaxation, not an alias here.
limitations: Optimality is over randomized predictors derived from the supplied binary prediction and group for the specified distribution and loss, not every possible predictor using raw features.
Fitting needs target labels and group information; deployment needs group membership. Empirical estimates and distribution changes can invalidate population parity.
The four-parameter statement assumes two groups and binary predictions; it does not assert that a general score-valued postprocessor has four parameters.
Equal conditional error rates do not establish equal accuracy, individual fairness or a universal fairness judgment. The printed proof is not reproduced as implementation code.
entries.mapping_rationale: Postprocesses binary classification decisions; the algorithm and the task are related at different abstraction levels, so this is not an equivalence or subclass assertion.
entries.abstract_interpretation: Proposes observable parity criteria and separate postprocessing constructions. This addition isolates the binary-predictor linear program, whose optimality concerns derived predictors and the specified distribution.

entries.title: Fairness Through Awareness
entries.version: arXiv:1104.3913v2, revised 2011-11-29; downloaded PDF title-page date 2024-11-26
entries.name: Fairness LP
entries.definition: A finite-population optimization procedure that assigns outcome distributions to individuals to minimize expected loss under pairwise Lipschitz similarity constraints, expressible as a linear program for the total-variation or relative-infinity distribution distances used by Dwork et al.
entries.mechanism: Choose a probability vector for each individual and minimize the supplied expected loss. Enforce normalization, nonnegativity and distribution distances bounded by the supplied task metric for every individual pair. Total-variation constraints admit a linear-program formulation; the relative-infinity choice yields pairwise linear probability-ratio bounds with fixed metric-dependent coefficients.
entries.locator: Section 2 and Section 2.1, Figure 1 equations (2)–(4), Lemmas 2.1–2.2 and Remark 2.1, PDF pp. 5–6 (printed pp. 4–5)
entries.identity_notes: The source names this optimization formulation Fairness LP. It is a procedure enforcing LipschitzIndividualFairness, not the criterion itself, a generic linear-program solver or a learned similarity metric. The two documented distribution-distance choices are retained as configurations of one formulation.
limitations: The individual metric and utility loss are inputs; solving the program does not establish that either is normatively appropriate.

The cited polynomial-size result concerns a finite set of individuals and outcomes with the specified distribution distances, not arbitrary metrics on output distributions or an unrestricted population.
Extrapolating from sampled individuals to unseen individuals is a separate challenge explicitly noted in Remark 2.1.
Individual constraints do not automatically imply demographic parity without additional assumptions about the population and metric.
entries.mapping_rationale: Computes a randomized classification assignment. Classification denotes the task, while this record denotes its constrained optimization procedure; MetricLearning instead learns representations and does not denote this supplied-metric program.
entries.abstract_interpretation: Proposes task-specific individual similarity and utility optimization subject to that requirement. The named finite Fairness LP is distinct from the criterion and depends on a supplied metric.

entries.title: Counterfactual Fairness
entries.name: FAIRLEARNING
entries.definition: A causal-model-dependent learning procedure that minimizes predictive loss averaged over inferred background variables, restricting the latent predictor to those variables and observed non-descendants of protected attributes.
entries.mechanism: Given a causal model and each training case, infer the posterior of background variables conditioned on observed features and protected attributes. Approximate the expected loss with MCMC samples when needed, expand the training cases with these latent samples, and fit a predictor using the sampled background variables and observed non-descendants. The paper reports predictions by posterior-averaging the fitted latent predictor for a new case.
entries.locator: Section 3.2 Lemma 1, Section 4.1 FAIRLEARNING pseudocode and prediction rule, Section 4.2 causal-model assumptions, PDF pp. 5–7
entries.identity_notes: The named training algorithm is distinct from CounterfactualFairness, the causal model supplied to it and any particular fitted predictor. The source distinguishes the latent predictor from its posterior-averaged reported prediction; this record preserves that distinction.
limitations: A causal model is an input, and compatible observed distributions need not identify its counterfactual assumptions.

Lemma 1 applies to functions of non-descendants in the posited model. This record does not turn that lemma into an unconditional guarantee for an arbitrary deployed posterior-mean predictor or a misspecified model.
Posterior inference and Monte Carlo or optimization approximations introduce computational and estimation dependencies; no exact finite-sample guarantee is asserted.
Protected attributes and descendant features can inform latent posterior inference even though the latent predictive function is restricted; excluding a raw feature alone is a different procedure.
entries.mapping_rationale: Requires a causal graphical model to infer background variables and identify non-descendants. It is a learning algorithm using the model, not a causal model family or an AIO subclass claim.
entries.abstract_interpretation: Proposes a causal fairness condition and a model-dependent latent learning algorithm. This addition retains the difference between the latent predictor and the reported posterior mean.

entries.title: The Sensitivity of Counterfactual Fairness to Unmeasured Confounding
entries.name: Bivariate counterfactual-fairness sensitivity analysis
entries.definition: A model-based sensitivity procedure that varies the correlation between two structural error terms and measures how a predictor built under an unconfounded additive-noise model changes on counterfactual data generated under the alternative confounded model.
entries.mechanism: Fit an unconfounded working model and a predictor of its residuals. At a selected error correlation, fit an alternative additive-noise model, retain its inferred errors while changing the protected attribute, and propagate the intervention through the causal ordering. Recompute residuals of these counterfactual features using the original working-model coefficients, apply the fixed original predictor and average squared prediction differences. Repeat across correlations to obtain a sensitivity curve.
entries.locator: Section 3, Tool #1: grid-based; Sections 3.1–3.4, equations (2)–(6), PDF pp. 3–6; Section 5, PDF p. 8 for grid use
entries.identity_notes: This record denotes the paper’s two-error grid-based sensitivity procedure. The mean squared discrepancy is its output, not another fairness criterion. The multivariate MAXCFU optimizer is separately represented because it searches a matrix of correlations with a different algorithm.
limitations: Alternative Model B is a hypothetical data-generating model, not an identified causal ground truth; the sensitivity parameter and acceptable discrepancy require domain judgment.
The inspected construction uses specified additive-noise structural functions, embeddings and Gaussian error covariance, rather than arbitrary hidden confounding.

Fitting, covariance invertibility and numerical grid resolution matter. The record does not certify a global maximum over all admissible models or extrapolate the source’s bivariate boundary statement to multiple error terms.
Squared prediction differences depend on the prediction scale and assessed sample; they are not automatically calibrated probabilities of discrimination or a universal fairness score.
entries.mapping_rationale: Evaluates predictor sensitivity using alternative causal graphical models and their counterfactuals. This evaluation procedure is not itself a causal model family or a type of bias.
entries.abstract_interpretation: Examines sensitivity to omitted confounding using additive-noise models, with a bivariate grid procedure and multivariate differentiable search. Abstract claims about maximum discrepancy are narrowed by the method’s covariance-validity and local-optimization limitations.

entries.title: The Sensitivity of Counterfactual Fairness to Unmeasured Confounding
entries.name: MAXCFU
entries.definition: A multivariate sensitivity algorithm that uses gradient ascent through fitted additive-noise models to search for large counterfactual prediction discrepancies under bounded correlations of structural error terms.
entries.mechanism: Fit the working model and its residual-based predictor once. Parameterize candidate error correlations through a transformed matrix product, fit the alternative model for each candidate, propagate counterfactual features, and measure squared prediction changes using the original predictor and working-model residual transform. Algorithm 1 uses minibatches and automatic differentiation to ascend this discrepancy with respect to the correlation parameters, then evaluates it on the full data.
entries.locator: Sections 4.1–4.3, equation (7) and Algorithm 1 MAXCFU, PDF pp. 6–8; Section 3.4 equation (6) for the discrepancy
entries.identity_notes: MAXCFU is the named optimization-based tool for multivariate confounding, distinct from the bivariate grid procedure, its CFU discrepancy and the counterfactual-fairness criterion. The record describes the published search procedure, not a certified optimizer.
limitations: The published off-diagonal tanh transformation gives a symmetric unit-diagonal matrix with bounded entries but explicitly does not guarantee positive semidefiniteness. A resulting matrix is therefore not automatically a valid correlation matrix.
Nested fitting and the outer search are nonconvex; local optimization, initialization and differentiation through fitting matter. No certified global worst-case value is asserted.
Sensitivity is conditional on the assumed structural model, predictor, intervention, confounding budget and sample. It does not identify the true hidden confounding or establish overall fairness.
The sparse clique parameterization is discussed but not exercised in the paper’s experiments, and its expressivity and numerical constraints are not certified here.
entries.mapping_rationale: Uses counterfactuals from parameterized causal graphical models to assess prediction sensitivity. The evaluation algorithm and the model class are related, without an equivalence or subclass assertion.
